decks.title: Genetics — Part 1: Terms, Mendel and the monohybrid cross
goals: Define the terms gene, allele, dominant, recessive, homozygous, heterozygous, phenotype, genotype, mutation and variation
State Mendel’s three laws and explain why he chose the garden pea
Work out a monohybrid cross to the F2 and derive the 3 : 1 and 1 : 2 : 1 ratios

slides.heading: Genetics
slides.body_md: Part 1 — the language of genetics, Mendel’s experiments and the monohybrid cross.

visual.alt: Flow from genes on chromosomes to alleles, to crosses and ratios, to the laws of inheritance

slides.narration: Why do children resemble their parents, yet differ from them and from one another? Genetics is the study of heredity and variation. We start with a few key words, then follow a monk’s experiments on garden peas.

slides.heading: Key terms

rows: Unit of heredity on a chromosome
One of the alternative forms of a gene
Shows its effect even in a single copy
Shows only when two copies are present

visual.alt: Table of eight genetic terms with meanings and pea examples

slides.narration: A gene for flower colour can exist in two forms, called alleles. The violet allele is dominant and the white one recessive. A plant with two identical alleles is homozygous; one with two different alleles is heterozygous. Genotype is the allele pair; phenotype is what you see.

slides.heading: Mutation and variation

rows: Differences among individuals of the same species
A sudden heritable change in a gene or chromosome; a source of new variation

visual.alt: Table defining variation and mutation

slides.narration: No two people, apart from identical twins, are genetically alike. Such differences are variations. Some arise from new mixtures of genes; others from mutations, sudden changes in the genetic material that can be passed on.

slides.heading: Quick check: two recessive alleles
slides.body_md: A pea plant with genotype vv is…
slides.narration: Are the two alleles alike or different, and which kind are they?

slides.heading: Why Mendel chose the garden pea

rows: Tall or dwarf, violet or white: easy to score
Large numbers in a short time

visual.alt: Table of features of the garden pea and why each helped Mendel

slides.narration: Gregor Mendel chose an ideal plant. Its characters come in clear pairs. It normally fertilises itself, so pure lines stay pure, yet he could cross plants by hand. And it grows quickly with many seeds, so he could count large numbers.

slides.narration: Write the gametes of one parent down the side and the other along the top. Fill each box by combining them. Three boxes have at least one violet allele, so three quarters are violet. One box has two white alleles.

slides.heading: Worked example 1: expected numbers
slides.body_md: 820 F2 plants from a Vv × Vv cross.
bullets: Step 1: find the fractions: violet three quarters, white one quarter.
Step 2: multiply by 820.
Step 3: check that the numbers add up.

visual.alt: Worked table: of eight hundred and twenty plants, six hundred and fifteen violet and two hundred and five white

slides.narration: Ratios become numbers by simple multiplication. Three quarters of eight hundred and twenty is six hundred and fifteen violet plants, and one quarter is two hundred and five white. Real counts come close to these, not exactly equal.

slides.heading: Mendel’s laws

rows: In a hybrid, only the dominant character shows
The two alleles separate at gamete formation; each gamete gets one
Alleles of different genes are distributed to gametes independently

visual.alt: Table of Mendel’s three laws with statements

slides.narration: Three laws came from these crosses. Dominance: the hybrid shows only one character. Segregation: alleles separate into gametes, so gametes are pure. Independent assortment, which we meet in Part two: different genes are sorted into gametes independently.

slides.heading: Quick check: violet F2 plants
slides.body_md: True or false: two of every three violet F2 plants are heterozygous.
slides.narration: Count the violet boxes and see how many are Vv.

slides.heading: Worked example 2: the test cross
slides.body_md: Is a violet plant VV or Vv? Cross it with white (vv).
bullets: Step 1: VV × vv gives all Vv: **all violet**.
Step 2: Vv × vv gives Vv and vv: **half white**.
Step 3: read the parent’s genotype from the offspring.

visual.alt: Worked table: a VV parent gives all violet offspring; a Vv parent gives half violet and half white

slides.narration: Because the white parent can give only white alleles, each offspring shows exactly which allele the violet parent passed on. Any white offspring prove the parent was heterozygous.

slides.heading: Quick check: the visible character
slides.body_md: Fill in: the visible expression of a character is its ______.
slides.narration: Genotype is the letters; this is what you see.

slides.heading: Summary
bullets: Alleles are forms of a gene; dominant shows in one copy, recessive needs two.
Genotype is the allele pair; phenotype is the visible character.
Monohybrid F2: 3 : 1 phenotypes, 1 : 2 : 1 genotypes.
Laws: dominance, segregation, independent assortment.

visual.alt: Summary table of three crosses and their results

slides.narration: To recap. Genes come in alleles. In a monohybrid cross the hybrid shows the dominant character, and the recessive one returns in a quarter of the second generation. A test cross with the recessive parent reveals a hidden genotype.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: Always write the **gametes** before the Punnett square.
Use a **capital** for the dominant allele and the **same letter, small,** for the recessive.
Give **both** ratios for a monohybrid F2.
State laws in full sentences.
slides.narration: Exam tips. Show the gametes, then the square. Use one letter in capital and small form for each gene. For a monohybrid cross, give both the phenotypic and genotypic ratios, and state each law as a full sentence.

slides.heading: Why males are affected more often

visual.alt: Table comparing males and females for an X-linked recessive allele

slides.narration: A boy has only one X. If it carries the faulty allele, nothing on the Y can mask it, so he is affected. A girl must inherit faulty alleles on both X chromosomes, which is rare, so most girls are only carriers.

visual.alt: Table of two colour-blindness crosses and their daughters and sons

slides.narration: Colour blindness is inherited in the same way. A colour blind father passes his X to every daughter, making them carriers, but never to his sons. A carrier mother passes the faulty X to half her sons, who are then colour blind.

slides.heading: Summary
bullets: Dihybrid F2: 9 : 3 : 3 : 1; two new combinations; independent assortment.
Females 44 + XX, males 44 + XY; the father’s sperm decides sex.
Haemophilia and colour blindness are X-linked recessive; males are affected more often.
Carrier mothers pass the allele to half their sons.

visual.alt: Summary table of the dihybrid ratio, sex determination and X-linked inheritance

slides.narration: To recap. Two genes assort independently, giving nine to three to three to one. A baby’s sex depends on the sperm. And recessive alleles on the X show up mainly in males, passed on through carrier mothers.

slides.heading: Exam tips
bullets: For a dihybrid cross give the **phenotypic ratio only**: the genotypic ratio is not in your syllabus.
In X-linked crosses, write alleles as **superscripts on X**; the Y carries none.
Answer "who decides sex?" with the **gametes of both parents**.
Say **carrier**, not "affected", for a heterozygous woman.

sections.heading: 1. Terms in genetics
sections.body_md:
**Genetics** is the study of heredity (passing of characters from parents to offspring) and variation.

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Gene** | A unit of heredity: a segment of DNA on a chromosome that controls a character |
| **Allele** | One of the alternative forms of a gene at the same position on homologous chromosomes (V and v) |
| **Dominant** | Allele that expresses itself in the presence of another allele (V) |
| **Recessive** | Allele that expresses itself only when both alleles are alike (vv) |
| **Homozygous** | Having two identical alleles (VV or vv); breeds true |
| **Heterozygous** | Having two different alleles (Vv); a hybrid |
| **Genotype** | The genetic make-up for a character (VV, Vv, vv) |
| **Phenotype** | The observable character (violet or white flowers) |
| **Mutation** | A sudden heritable change in a gene or chromosome |
| **Variation** | Differences among individuals of the same species |

key_terms.definition_md: An alternative form of a gene.
The genetic make-up for a character.

visual.alt: Table of three genotypes for flower colour and their phenotypes

sections.heading: 2. Mendel and his laws
sections.body_md:
**Gregor Johann Mendel** studied inheritance in the **garden pea** (*Pisum sativum*). He chose it because it has **clearly contrasting characters**, is **self-pollinating** (pure lines) yet can be **cross-pollinated by hand**, and has a **short life cycle** with **many seeds**.

**Law of dominance:** when two contrasting alleles are present, only the **dominant** one is expressed in the hybrid.

**Law of segregation (purity of gametes):** the two alleles of a gene **separate** during gamete formation, so each gamete receives **only one** allele.

**Law of independent assortment:** alleles of **different genes** are distributed to gametes **independently** of one another (seen in a dihybrid cross).

key_terms.definition_md: Alleles separate at gamete formation; each gamete is pure.
Alleles of different genes are distributed independently.

sections.heading: 5. Sex determination in human beings
sections.body_md:
Human body cells have **23 pairs** of chromosomes: **22 pairs of autosomes** and **one pair of sex chromosomes**.
- Female: **44 + XX**; all eggs **22 + X** (homogametic).
- Male: **44 + XY**; sperms **22 + X** or **22 + Y** in equal numbers (heterogametic).

X sperm + egg → **44 + XX, girl**; Y sperm + egg → **44 + XY, boy**. So the **father’s gamete** decides the sex, and the chance of a boy or a girl is **one half** at every birth.

The X and Y chromosomes that determine sex.

sections.heading: 6. X-linked inheritance: haemophilia and colour blindness
sections.body_md:
Genes carried on the **X chromosome** are **X-linked**. The alleles for **haemophilia** (blood fails to clot) and **red–green colour blindness** are **recessive**.
- **Male (XY):** one faulty X → **affected** (no matching allele on Y).
- **Female (XX):** one faulty X → **carrier** (normal); two faulty X → affected (rare).

**Carrier mother × normal father:** daughters half normal, half carriers; **sons half normal, half affected**.
**Affected father × normal mother:** **all daughters carriers**; **all sons normal** (sons get his Y).

So X-linked disorders are **commoner in males** and pass from a **carrier mother to her sons** (criss-cross inheritance).

key_terms.definition_md: A heterozygous person who carries a recessive allele without showing it.
An X-linked disorder in which blood does not clot normally.
An X-linked disorder in which red and green cannot be told apart.

**Common mistakes**
- Writing the genotypic ratio for a dihybrid F2 (not in the syllabus) or giving 3 : 1 for it.

- Calling a heterozygous woman "affected" instead of a **carrier**.
- Putting X-linked alleles on the Y chromosome.

- 1 mark: a term, a genotype, a ratio, an odd one out with its category.
- 2 marks: a law stated with evidence, or two reasons.
- 3 marks: a cross — parents and gametes, Punnett square, and correct ratios or conclusions.

questions.solution_md: Differences among members of a species are variations; mutation is only one of their sources — option (a).

questions.stem_md: Give the biological term: an organism with two different alleles of a gene, such as Vv.

answer.model_answer_md: **Heterozygous** (a hybrid).

questions.solution_md: Heterozygous.

questions.stem_md: Give the biological term: the genetic make-up of an organism for a character, written with letters such as Tt.

answer.model_answer_md: **Genotype.**

questions.solution_md: Genotype.

questions.stem_md: Give the biological term: the allele that shows its effect even when only one copy is present.

answer.model_answer_md: **Dominant** allele.

questions.solution_md: Dominant.

questions.stem_md: Choose the odd one out and name the category to which the other three belong: TT, Tt, tt, Tall.

answer.model_answer_md: **Tall**; the others are **genotypes** (Tall is a phenotype).

questions.solution_md: Tall is a phenotype.

questions.stem_md: The visible expression of a character, such as white flowers, is its ______.
questions.solution_md: Phenotype.

questions.stem_md: Which feature of the garden pea made it suitable for Mendel’s experiments?

options.text_md: It takes several years to flower
It has many clearly contrasting characters and is normally self-pollinating
It has only one pair of chromosomes
It cannot be cross-pollinated by hand

questions.solution_md: Pea has sharply contrasting traits, a short life cycle, many seeds and natural self-pollination, yet can be crossed by hand — option (b).

questions.stem_md: When Mendel crossed pure violet-flowered plants with pure white-flowered plants, all the F1 plants were violet. This illustrates the law of
questions.solution_md: Only the dominant character appears in the F1 hybrid — law of dominance, option (c).

questions.stem_md: White flowers, absent in the F1, reappear in the F2. Which law explains this?

options.text_md: Law of dominance: the dominant allele always shows
Law of independent assortment: two characters are inherited separately
Law of segregation: the two alleles separate when gametes form
Law of mutation: new alleles appear in the F2

questions.solution_md: The recessive allele, hidden in the F1, separates into some gametes and two such gametes give vv in the F2 — option (c).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Gametes are always pure for a character.

**Reason (R):** Each gamete receives only one allele of each gene.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

questions.solution_md: Both are true, and because each gamete carries just one allele, it is pure for that character (law of segregation) — option (c).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** In a dihybrid cross, new combinations such as tall white and dwarf violet appear in the F2.

**Reason (R):** The alleles of height and flower colour are always inherited together.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

questions.solution_md: The assertion is true. The reason is false: the two genes assort independently, which is why new combinations appear — option (a).

questions.stem_md: State Mendel’s law of segregation and give one observation from a violet × white cross that supports it.

answer.model_answer_md: **Law of segregation:** the two alleles of a gene **separate** during gamete formation, so each gamete gets **only one** allele. **Evidence:** white flowers, **absent in the F1**, **reappear** in a quarter of the F2.

questions.solution_md: Statement and evidence.

questions.stem_md: Give two reasons why Mendel chose the garden pea for his experiments.

answer.model_answer_md:
1. It has many **pairs of clearly contrasting characters** (tall/dwarf, violet/white flowers).
2. It is **self-pollinating**, so pure lines are easy to keep, yet it can be **cross-pollinated by hand**; it also has a **short life cycle** with many seeds.

questions.solution_md: Contrasting traits; self-pollination; short life cycle; many seeds.

questions.stem_md: Choose the odd one out and name the category to which the other three belong: Dominance, Segregation, Independent assortment, Crossing over.

answer.model_answer_md: **Crossing over**; the others are **Mendel’s laws of inheritance**.

questions.solution_md: Crossing over is an event of meiosis.

questions.stem_md: Two heterozygous violet-flowered plants (Vv) are crossed. The phenotypic ratio of the offspring will be
questions.solution_md: Vv × Vv gives VV, Vv, Vv, vv: 3 : 1 — option (d).

questions.stem_md: What fraction of the F2 plants from a Vv × Vv cross will be pure-breeding violet (VV)?
questions.solution_md: VV is 1 of the 4 boxes — option (b).

questions.stem_md: A tall pea plant crossed with a dwarf plant gives about equal numbers of tall and dwarf offspring. The genotype of the tall parent is

options.text_md: TT or Tt; it cannot be told

questions.solution_md: Only Tt × tt gives tall and dwarf in a 1 : 1 ratio; TT × tt would give all tall — option (a).

questions.stem_md: An F1 violet-flowered plant (Vv) is self-pollinated and 820 seeds grow into plants. How many are expected to have white flowers?
questions.solution_md: White is $\tfrac{1}{4}$ of the F2: $\tfrac{1}{4} \times 820 = 205$ (and 615 violet).

questions.stem_md: True or false? In a monohybrid F2 generation, two out of every three violet-flowered plants are heterozygous.
questions.solution_md: True. Among violet plants (VV, Vv, Vv), two of three are Vv.

questions.stem_md: A pure tall pea plant (TT) is crossed with a pure dwarf plant (tt). Using a Punnett square, work out the F1 and F2 generations and state the F2 phenotypic and genotypic ratios.

answer.model_answer_md: **F1:** TT × tt gives gametes T and t, so all offspring are **Tt (tall)**. **F2:** Tt × Tt gives TT, Tt, Tt, tt. **Phenotypic ratio 3 tall : 1 dwarf**; **genotypic ratio 1 TT : 2 Tt : 1 tt**.

questions.solution_md: F1 all Tt tall; F2 3 : 1 and 1 : 2 : 1.

questions.stem_md: How would you find out whether a violet-flowered pea plant is VV or Vv? Explain the expected results.

answer.model_answer_md: Do a **test cross**: cross it with a **white (vv)** plant. If **all** offspring are violet, the plant is **VV**; if about **half are white**, it is **Vv**.

questions.solution_md: Test cross with the recessive.

questions.solution_md: Two genes assorting independently give 9 : 3 : 3 : 1 — option (d).

questions.solution_md: The parents were tall violet and dwarf white, so tall white and dwarf violet are recombinations — option (b).

questions.solution_md: Dwarf violet (ttV_) occupies 3 of the 16 boxes — option (a).

questions.stem_md: A dihybrid F1 plant (TtVv) is selfed and gives 640 F2 plants. How many are expected to be tall with violet flowers?
questions.solution_md: Tall violet is $\tfrac{9}{16}$: $\tfrac{9}{16} \times 640 = 360$ (tall white 120, dwarf violet 120, dwarf white 40).

questions.stem_md: Explain how the F2 of a dihybrid cross (TTVV × ttvv) shows the law of independent assortment. State the phenotypes and the expected numbers among 640 F2 plants.

answer.model_answer_md: The F1 (TtVv) forms **four kinds of gametes** (TV, Tv, tV, tv) in equal numbers because the two genes **assort independently**. The F2 has **four phenotypes**: tall violet **360**, tall white **120**, dwarf violet **120**, dwarf white **40** (9 : 3 : 3 : 1); **two are new combinations**.

questions.solution_md: Four gamete types; 9:3:3:1 numbers; recombinants.

questions.stem_md: True or false? In a dihybrid F2, one plant in every sixteen shows both recessive characters.
questions.solution_md: True. The double recessive (ttvv) is 1 of 16.

questions.stem_md: Give the biological term: a cross in which the inheritance of two pairs of contrasting characters is studied together.

answer.model_answer_md: **Dihybrid cross.**

questions.solution_md: Dihybrid cross.

questions.stem_md: The sex of a human baby is decided by

options.text_md: whether the egg carries an X or a Y chromosome
the number of autosomes in the egg
whether the sperm that fertilises the egg carries an X or a Y chromosome

questions.solution_md: All eggs carry X; sperms carry X or Y, so the father’s gamete decides — option (d).

questions.stem_md: A human sperm cell normally contains
questions.solution_md: Gametes are haploid: 22 + X or 22 + Y — option (a).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** The mother determines the sex of the child.

**Reason (R):** All the eggs produced by a woman carry an X chromosome.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

questions.solution_md: The assertion is false: the father’s sperm (X or Y) determines the sex. The reason is true — option (b).

questions.stem_md: A couple already has three daughters. What is the probability (as a percentage) that their next child will be a son?
questions.solution_md: Each child is independent: half the sperms carry Y, so the chance is 1/2 = 50 percent.

questions.stem_md: True or false? A man produces two kinds of sperm, those with an X chromosome and those with a Y chromosome, in equal numbers.
questions.solution_md: True. Being XY, he forms X-bearing and Y-bearing sperms in a 1 : 1 ratio.

questions.stem_md: Give reason: there is an equal chance of a boy or a girl at every birth.

answer.model_answer_md: A father makes **X-bearing and Y-bearing sperms in equal numbers**, and the egg always carries **X**. So fertilisation by either kind is **equally likely**, giving XX (girl) or XY (boy).

questions.solution_md: Equal X and Y sperms.

marking_scheme.step: Egg always X; XX vs XY

questions.stem_md: Give the biological term: the 22 pairs of chromosomes in a human body cell that are not concerned with sex.

answer.model_answer_md: **Autosomes.**

questions.solution_md: Autosomes.

questions.stem_md: A woman with normal blood clotting whose father had haemophilia is most likely to be

options.text_md: a carrier, with one normal and one faulty X chromosome
completely free of the haemophilia allele
able to pass haemophilia only to her daughters

questions.solution_md: She received her father’s only X, which carries the haemophilia allele, but her mother’s normal X masks it — option (a).

questions.stem_md: Why is colour blindness more common in men than in women?

options.text_md: The allele is on the Y chromosome
The allele is dominant in men and recessive in women
Men have only one X chromosome, so a single recessive allele shows its effect

questions.solution_md: In males the X has no partner allele to mask it — option (d).

questions.stem_md: A colour-blind man marries a woman who carries no colour-blindness allele. What can be said of their sons?

options.text_md: All will have normal vision, because sons get their X from the mother

questions.solution_md: Sons get Y from the father and a normal X from the mother — option (c).

questions.stem_md:
**Assertion (A):** Haemophilia is very rare in women.

**Reason (R):** A woman shows haemophilia only if both her X chromosomes carry the recessive allele.

Choose the correct option.

options.text_md: Both (A) and (R) are true, and (R) is the correct explanation of (A).
Both (A) and (R) are true, but (R) is not the correct explanation of (A).

questions.solution_md: Both are true, and the need for two faulty X chromosomes explains why affected women are rare — option (c).

questions.stem_md: Give the biological term: a person who has a recessive disease-causing allele but does not show the disease.

answer.model_answer_md: **Carrier.**

questions.solution_md: Carrier.

questions.stem_md: Give reason: haemophilia is called a "bleeder’s disease".

answer.model_answer_md: Blood of a haemophilic person **does not clot normally**, so even a small cut may **bleed for a long time**.

questions.solution_md: Clotting fails.

questions.stem_md: Choose the odd one out and name the category to which the other three belong (H = normal clotting, h = haemophilia): $X^hY$, $X^HX^h$, $X^HY$, $X^HX^H$.

answer.model_answer_md: $X^hY$; the others **clot their blood normally** (they do not suffer from haemophilia).

questions.solution_md: XhY is a haemophilic male.

questions.stem_md: Explain why a haemophilic father never passes haemophilia to his sons.

answer.model_answer_md: A father gives his **Y chromosome** to his sons and his **X** to his daughters. The haemophilia allele is on the **X**, so his sons receive his Y and **cannot** get the allele from him; all his daughters become **carriers**.

questions.solution_md: Sons get his Y.

questions.stem_md: A carrier woman marries a man with normal blood clotting. With a cross, show the possible children and state the chance of a haemophilic son.

answer.model_answer_md: Mother $X^HX^h$ × father $X^HY$. Gametes: $X^H$, $X^h$ and $X^H$, $Y$. Children: $X^HX^H$ **normal daughter**, $X^HX^h$ **carrier daughter**, $X^HY$ **normal son**, $X^hY$ **haemophilic son**. Chance of a haemophilic son = **1 in 4** (25 percent) of all children.

questions.solution_md: Haemophilic son 25 percent of all children.

questions.stem_md: Genes for haemophilia and colour blindness are carried on the ______ chromosome.
questions.solution_md: X.

answer.model_answer_md: The allele is **recessive**; her other X carries the **dominant normal allele (C)**, which **masks** it.

children.stem_md: Name the chromosome on which the colour-blindness gene lies.

answer.model_answer_md: The **X chromosome**.

questions.stem_md: A pure tall pea plant (TT) is crossed with a pure dwarf plant (tt). The F1 plants will be

options.text_md: of medium height, with genotype Tt

questions.solution_md: Every F1 plant gets T from one parent and t from the other: Tt, tall because T is dominant — option (c).

questions.stem_md: A colour-blind woman marries a man with normal vision. Which statement about their children is correct?

options.text_md: All children will have normal vision
Only daughters will be colour blind
All sons will be colour blind and all daughters will be carriers
Half the sons and half the daughters will be colour blind

questions.solution_md: Every son gets one of her faulty X chromosomes; every daughter also gets the father’s normal X, which masks the allele — option (c).

questions.stem_md: True or false? A mutation in a body (skin) cell is passed on to the person’s children.
questions.solution_md: False. Only mutations in the cells that form gametes can be inherited; a skin-cell mutation is not passed on.

questions.stem_md: Differentiate between a dominant and a recessive allele, giving one example of each from pea flower colour.

answer.model_answer_md: A **dominant** allele shows its effect even when **only one copy** is present, as **V (violet)** in Vv. A **recessive** allele shows its effect only when **both copies** are present, as **v (white)** in vv.
